high_priority_articles.summary: Global Market: BoE's Huw Pill wary of market bets on four rate hikes over next year  The Economic Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Pill, who voted in favour of raising interest rates at the central bank's September meeting, said it was not yet clear whether borrowing costs would need to rise by as much as financial markets anticipate. He made the remarks at an event organised by Citi on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund's semi-annual meetings in Bangkok, Reuters reported.
Read more: Global Market: China’s yuan firms as investors await US CPI data, assess inflation
Pill said the central bank needed to ensure monetary policy was positioned appropriately to address inflationary pressures, while questioning whether four rate increases would be warranted over the coming 12 months.
The comments highlight divisions within the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee over the appropriate response to the energy shock stemming from the Iran war. Pill and two other MPC members voted for a rate increase in September, while the majority, including Governor Andrew Bailey, favoured keeping rates unchanged until there was greater clarity on the conflict's economic impact, Reuters reported.
Bailey reiterated on Tuesday that the energy shock had so far had a limited effect on broader inflationary pressures in the UK. However, he warned that the longer the disruption continued, the greater the risk that its effects would spread more widely through the economy.

While financial markets have priced in a series of rate increases over the coming year, Pill's remarks suggest policymakers remain divided over the scale and timing of any further tightening, with the outlook likely to depend on how the energy shock evolves and whether it generates more persistent inflationary pressures.

high_priority_articles.title: Euro-to-Dollar Pressure Builds as U.S. Core Inflation Pressures Fed Into Action - Pound Sterling Live
high_priority_articles.summary: Euro-to-Dollar Pressure Builds as U.S. Core Inflation Pressures Fed Into Action  Pound Sterling Live
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Image © Adobe Images
Hotter underlying US price growth has pushed the single currency to a fresh 17-month low, and strategists see the dollar's rate support strengthening.
The Euro to Dollar exchange rate fell to a fresh 17-month low after US core inflation beat expectations, reviving bets on another Federal Reserve rate hike this month.
Core consumer prices, which strip out food and energy, rose 0.3% in September against a consensus of 0.2%, lifting the annual core rate to 2.6%.
Headline inflation rose 0.6% on the month, in line with forecasts, taking the annual rate to 3.7% as gasoline prices climbed.
Hotter core inflation matters more for the Fed than the energy-driven headline, because it shows price pressures spreading into the wider economy; a Fed that hikes again widens the US interest rate advantage and pulls capital towards the dollar.
"Underlying consumer prices rose more quickly than expected in the United States last month, strengthening the case for more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, and lifting the dollar," says Karl Schamotta, Chief Market Strategist at Corpay.
EUR/USD fell from 1.1199 before the release to 1.1138 within 15 minutes, a drop of 0.5% that broke through Monday's 1.1154 low.
Schamotta says traders are sharply raising the odds of an October hike, and Treasury yields are rising at the policy-sensitive end of the curve.
New York Fed President John Williams had argued only on Tuesday that one more hike this year would be enough, a view that sent the odds of an October move down to around 20%.
"A stronger-than-expected core inflation reading adds to mounting evidence that domestic price pressures are becoming more entrenched, rather than easing," says George Brown, Senior Economist at Schroders.
Brown says markets are right to expect much tighter policy, and the open question is whether the Fed will deliver it.
Richard Carter, Head of Fixed Interest Research at Quilter Cheviot, says another hike this year cannot be ruled out and ten-year Treasury yields could keep rising.
What's Next for EUR/USD
The case for a limited move rests on how much Fed tightening was already priced before the data.
Societe Generale's Kit Juckes said in a recent update that market pricing for the Fed Funds rate stood just below 5%, already above the highest forecast in the Bloomberg survey, and that only a core reading well above consensus would lift it further.
Corpay expects some of today's dollar gains to fade, though Schamotta says the Fed's calculus has shifted.
"We suspect this knee-jerk reaction could fade somewhat, but there's no question that the monetary tightening calculus has shifted," he says.
Positioning adds to the case for a bounce, with Societe Generale reporting euro short positions at their highest since December 2024, but the technical targets sit lower:
• Support at 1.1115, UOB's one-to-three-week target
• Support at 1.11, the area ING and KBC both flag
• Resistance at 1.1154, Monday's low, now overhead
• Resistance at 1.1220, the level UOB says would confirm the decline has stabilised
"A test of 1.110 remains the risk for EUR/USD," says Francesco Pesole, FX Strategist at ING.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at the IMF on Friday, the next chance for policymakers to confirm or push back on the October hike pricing that today's data rebuilt.
A daily close back above 1.1154 would mark today's break as a false one; failing that, 1.1115 and then 1.11 are the next stops.

high_priority_articles.title: US inflation to hit 3.6% in September? Why CPI data matters for Fed rate decision | Hindustan Times - Hindustan Times
high_priority_articles.summary: US inflation to hit 3.6% in September? Why CPI data matters for Fed rate decision | Hindustan Times  Hindustan Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US inflation may rise to 3.6% in September as gas prices climb. The CPI report could shape the Fed's October rate decision and rate hike outlook.
The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, due on Wednesday, October 15, is expected to show that inflation increased in September as energy prices rose. The data will help investors understand how prices are changing and what the Federal Reserve may do with interest rates.
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect annual US inflation to increase to 3.6% in September, up from 3.4% in August. This would mean that consumer prices are rising faster than they did a year earlier. Consumer prices are forecast to rise 0.6% in September compared with August. This would be faster than the 0.4% monthly increase recorded in August.
US inflation rises as gas prices hit record high
Gasoline prices are expected to be a major reason for the rise in US inflation in September. When fuel prices go up, travelling becomes more expensive. It also costs more to make and deliver goods.
According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of gasoline in the US reached a record $4.33 per gallon last month. This was nearly 50 cents higher than the previous monthly record set in 2023.
US core inflation rate expected to rise to 2.5%
Core inflation does not include food and energy prices because they can change quickly. It is expected to rise slightly in September.
Also read: US Treasury yields today: 10-year yield falls as oil prices drop ahead of inflation data
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the annual core inflation rate to increase to 2.5% in September, up from 2.4% in August. Core consumer prices are also expected to rise by 0.2% from August to September. This would be lower than the higher-than-expected 0.3% increase recorded in August.
Core inflation is an important measure for Federal Reserve officials because it excludes food and energy prices, which can be volatile. The September reading will help policymakers assess whether underlying price pressures are easing or remaining high.
Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said the September CPI report is expected to be relatively straightforward. However, he warned that the absence of a major surprise does not mean the inflation problem has been solved, as price pressures remain elevated, according to Yahoo Finance.
Fed rate decision: Will interest rates stay unchanged?
If core inflation comes in around economists' expectations, the Federal Reserve may have enough reason to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 28 meeting. Policymakers will also consider other economic data before making their decision.
The September jobs report showed that the US added only 29,000 jobs, while the unemployment rate increased. This relatively weak employment data is another factor that could influence the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision.
Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials have been mixed, particularly over when rates might need to change again. Their comments reflect the challenge of bringing inflation down without putting too much pressure on the economy.
Traders currently see a 76% chance that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting. This expectation reflects the latest economic data and comments from central bank officials.
Also read: US bank earnings: JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Citi show consumers remain resilient despite high rates
US inflation risks: Airfares, hotels and diesel prices
Economists warn that core inflation could rise more than expected. Higher costs for services and other goods could prevent inflation from slowing, making it harder for the Federal Reserve to bring price increases under control.
Rising costs for air travel, hotels and auto parts are among the factors economists are watching. If these costs increase faster than expected, they could push core inflation higher in September. Diesel fuel is widely used to transport goods. A sharp increase in diesel prices can make shipping and distribution more expensive, potentially pushing up prices for businesses and consumers.
October Fed rate hike back in focus as inflation stays high
Economists at RBC, led by Mike Reid, said there is still a limited chance of a major slowdown in core inflation. They also warned that September's CPI report may not fully reflect the risks that could push inflation higher in the coming months, according to Yahoo Finance.
If core inflation remains elevated for a second consecutive month, an interest rate hike in October could become a possibility again. This would depend on the inflation figures and the Federal Reserve's wider assessment of the economy.
Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau said a monthly core CPI increase of 0.3% would likely bring back speculation that the Federal Reserve may need to continue raising interest rates in October. Such a reading would be higher than the 0.2% increase currently expected, according to Yahoo Finance.
Why inflation data matters for the Fed
The report will help show whether inflation is moving closer to the Federal Reserve's goal or remains too high. If core inflation matches expectations, the Fed may keep rates unchanged. However, a stronger-than-expected reading could increase pressure on policymakers to consider another rate hike.

While Chief Economist Huw Pill said on Wednesday that the BOE should have acted sooner to tackle the energy shock caused by the Iran war, he added that more concrete evidence was needed before a bigger rise in rates.
"Is it obvious that we will need to follow market pricing to four 25 basis point hikes and so forth? There I would be a little bit more skeptical," he said at an event in Bangkok, where he's attending annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. "To get to 100 basis points, then I do think we probably need to see some more concrete manifestation of these risks."
Pill has been in the minority on the Monetary Policy Committee backing an immediate rate hike since April, shortly after the US and Israeli attacks on Iran rattled energy markets. Most BOE officials have held off action so far, believing that a tepid labor market and sharp tightening in financial conditions since the Middle Eastern conflict broke out have bought them time to assess the risk of high inflation persisting.
However, more UK officials are now edging toward support for an increase in borrowing costs.
In an interview with CNN late on Tuesday, Governor Andrew Bailey reiterated that it is becoming harder to avoid a rate hike, the longer the energy shock drags on.
Markets are pricing in a near-100% chance of the MPC voting for their first increase in bank rate in over three years at their November meeting. Traders then expect the BOE to back a further three quarter-point hikes by next summer. But Pill suggested he is reluctant to support a series of rate rises yet, given scant evidence on whether the energy shock is spreading widely across the economy.
"We will get more evidence, I think, over the next six-nine months around, for example, second round effects, which I would emphasize in my thinking are key to whether a shock to inflation becomes a more self-sustaining, persistent dynamic in inflation," he said.
Pill pointed to a more resilient UK economy and labor market as important factors, arguing that holding off action in response to uncertainty is a "little bit misguided."

Gold Recovers as Dollar and Bond Yields Retreat; Markets Await US Inflation Test
EghtesadOnline :Global markets reversed part of Monday’s moves ahead of Wednesday’s US inflation report. Oil prices fell on expectations of increased Russian diesel supplies and Saudi Arabia’s pipeline expansion, while investors turned their attention to bank earnings, inflation and the outlook for monetary policy.
Spot gold rose approximately 0.24% from the previous close to around $4,181.60 per ounce. The weaker dollar, lower oil prices and declining bond yields supported gold. Lower bond yields reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold, making the precious metal more attractive to investors.
However, inflation figures above expectations could revive the possibility of interest-rate increases and weaken this support.
Oil: Expectations of Higher Supply Counter Risks to Exports
Oil prices retreated after Monday’s surge. Reuters and The Wall Street Journal identified the prospect of increased Russian diesel supplies as a factor easing concerns about fuel shortages. However, damage to Russian refineries has cast doubt on whether those additional supplies can materialize as promised.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has announced plans to increase the export capacity of its pipeline network. Temporarily converting a gas pipeline could increase oil transportation capacity by 1.2 million barrels per day within seven to eight weeks. The plan matters for the outlook for exports, but the additional capacity has not yet translated into actual oil supplies reaching the market and has so far had only a temporary effect on prices.
The Dollar and Foreign Exchange Markets
The US Dollar Index fell approximately 0.24% on Tuesday to 102.33, retreating from the 18-month high it reached on Monday. Safe-haven demand and concerns about the Middle East had supported the dollar’s gains on Monday. Lower oil prices and renewed attention to the interest-rate outlook shifted its direction on Tuesday.
The euro rose approximately 0.24% to $1.11818, although concerns over France’s debt and budget outlook continue to weigh on its prospects.
In its analysis published on Tuesday, ING said markets had almost fully priced in a European Central Bank rate hike in December, leaving limited room for further support for the euro from that prospect.
The bank lowered its EUR/USD forecast for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027 to 1.13. It also continued to identify a possible test of the 1.11 level in the short term.
ING also expects EUR/GBP to trade within a range of 0.84 to 0.85 over the coming months. France’s difficulties and the possibility of further UK interest-rate increases are factors supporting the pound.
However, the bank considers market expectations for the scale of rate increases in 2027 to be excessive. The UK budget on October 28 is another risk on the horizon, although ING does not currently expect it to have a lasting negative effect on the pound.
Japan: October Rate Hike Pause Becomes More Likely
According to Bloomberg, Bank of Japan officials are reluctant to raise interest rates at two consecutive meetings and are therefore likely to pause at their October 30 meeting.
Policymakers want to assess the effects of September’s rate increase before making another move. A further increase in December remains possible, however, and the final decision has not yet been made.
Concerns Over US Equities
US cash markets had not yet opened on Tuesday. On Monday, the S&P 500 closed down 0.06% at 7,807.24, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.44% to 27,245.90.
Reports of progress by Chinese company CXMT have heightened concerns about competition and pressure on the profits of US chipmakers. Selling pressure has also spread to Asian markets, as investors worry that heavy investment in artificial intelligence may fail to generate sufficient returns in an environment of elevated interest rates.
Treasury Yields and the Federal Reserve
The US Treasury market has followed two different paths over the past week. Between October 6 and October 13, the yield on one-month Treasury bills rose from 3.943% to 4.042%, an increase of 9.9 basis points. Yields on three-month, six-month and one-year securities also increased by 3.9, 4.4 and 2.1 basis points, respectively.
From the two-year maturity onward, however, yields declined. The two-year Treasury yield fell 2.8 basis points to 4.77%, while the three-year yield dropped 3.2 basis points to 4.892%. The declines were greater for five-year and seven-year Treasuries, at 5.8 and 7.2 basis points, respectively.
The largest pullbacks occurred in longer-dated bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 9.2 basis points to 5.194%, the 20-year yield declined 10 basis points to 5.602%, and the 30-year yield dropped 10.3 basis points to 5.558%.
As a result, the spread between the 10-year and two-year Treasury yields narrowed from 48.8 to 42.4 basis points, indicating a flattening of the yield curve.
In Tuesday’s trading, The Wall Street Journal identified lower oil prices and declines in AI-related stocks as factors boosting demand for Treasuries and pushing yields down.
Reuters, citing Saxo Bank, reported that elevated yields in recent weeks had attracted buyers back into the bond market. However, persistent inflation, high oil prices and heavy government borrowing continue to stand in the way of a sustained recovery.
Wednesday’s inflation report will be an important test of whether the decline in yields can continue.
FedWatch puts the probability of the Federal Reserve holding rates steady at its October 28 meeting at 80.6%, compared with a 19.4% probability of a rate increase. The probability of a hike is 1.6 percentage points lower than on Monday.
What Are Markets Waiting For?
Earnings reports from major banks on Tuesday and the US Consumer Price Index (CPI) report on Wednesday are the most important tests ahead.
On Thursday, markets will receive the Producer Price Index (PPI), retail sales figures and oil inventory data. On Friday, remarks by Kevin Warsh could provide further clarity on how investors interpret the outlook for monetary policy.

high_priority_articles.title: Why Is China Warning Taiwan Over a Water Cannon Incident in the South China Sea? - Modern Diplomacy
high_priority_articles.summary: Why Is China Warning Taiwan Over a Water Cannon Incident in the South China Sea?  Modern Diplomacy
high_priority_articles.full_text:
China has warned Taiwan that it must “bear the consequences” of using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas Islands in the South China Sea, escalating tensions as Taipei reports increased Chinese military activity around the island.
The incident occurred earlier this month when a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel used a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat that allegedly failed to respond to warnings to leave restricted waters near the Taiwan-controlled islands.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard said the fishing boat subsequently suffered engine failure and was towed away by a nearby Chinese vessel.
Chen Binhua, spokesperson for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said Beijing had “indisputable sovereignty” over the Pratas Islands and surrounding waters. He described Chinese vessels operating in the area as acting legally and said Beijing would protect the lives and property of Chinese citizens.
Chen accused Taiwan of treating mainland vessels in a dangerous and aggressive manner, claiming that its actions were deliberately escalating cross-strait tensions. He warned that Taiwan would have to accept the consequences but did not specify what measures China might take.
A Taiwanese official with direct knowledge of the situation told Reuters that the Coast Guard had conducted normal law enforcement and responded carefully and proportionately to the incident.
Why the Pratas Islands Matter to China and Taiwan
The Pratas Islands lie between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong and are controlled by Taipei. Their location makes them strategically significant in the broader dispute between China and Taiwan.
The islands are more than 400 kilometres (250 miles) from Taiwan, leaving them geographically exposed to potential Chinese military pressure. Security experts consider them vulnerable to a Chinese attack because of their distance from Taiwan’s main territory.
The islands are designated as a national park and contain an airstrip but have no permanent civilian population.
Beijing claims democratically governed Taiwan as part of China and rejects all Taiwanese sovereignty claims, including those concerning the Pratas Islands. Taipei rejects Beijing’s territorial claims and maintains control over the islands.
Chinese coast guard vessels have increased patrols in the surrounding waters, adding another layer of tension to an already sensitive maritime environment.
Taiwan Warns of Growing Chinese ‘Grey Zone’ Tactics
The latest confrontation comes as Taiwan warns that China is expanding its use of so-called grey zone tactics, which involve coercive activities below the threshold of open military conflict.
Speaking at a forum in Taipei, Lii Wen, deputy secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, said Beijing was using a broader range of vessels, including maritime militia boats and research ships, to carry out what he described as incremental acts of aggression.
Lii warned that these activities could disrupt transportation and threaten critical infrastructure without triggering a conventional military response.
Grey zone operations can include coast guard patrols, maritime militia deployments, airspace incursions and other forms of sustained pressure. Such tactics can challenge Taiwan’s ability to enforce its jurisdiction while making it more difficult to determine when a response might escalate into a wider confrontation.
Beijing rejects Taiwan’s characterisation of its activities as aggression and maintains that its actions around the island are legitimate.
Chinese Military Activity Adds to Regional Tensions
Taiwan’s defence ministry reported another Chinese “joint combat readiness patrol” near the island on Wednesday, involving 13 aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets, alongside an unspecified number of Chinese navy vessels.
China’s defence ministry separately said the aircraft carrier Liaoning and accompanying ships were conducting drills in the Western Pacific. It did not provide further details about the exercises.
The military activity highlights the broader security pressures facing Taiwan as maritime confrontations continue around its outlying islands.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard, rather than its military, is responsible for day-to-day security around the Pratas Islands. This distinction is important because encounters involving civilian or law enforcement vessels can create diplomatic and security tensions without immediately becoming direct military confrontations.
What Happens Next?
The water cannon incident could become another flashpoint in relations across the Taiwan Strait, particularly if China responds by increasing coast guard patrols or deploying additional vessels near the Pratas Islands.
For Beijing, challenging Taiwan’s authority over the surrounding waters reinforces its rejection of Taiwanese sovereignty. For Taipei, allowing Chinese vessels to operate in restricted waters without enforcement could undermine its ability to maintain control over territory it administers.
The immediate question is whether China will limit its response to political warnings or use the incident to justify more persistent maritime activity around the islands.
Any increase in patrols or confrontations could raise the risk of miscalculation, particularly as Chinese military operations around Taiwan continue. Even without open conflict, repeated encounters between coast guard vessels, fishing boats and other maritime actors could intensify pressure on Taiwan and complicate efforts to maintain stability across the Taiwan Strait.

After the Cold War, NATO was reconceived as a “cooperative-security” organization whose mandate was to include two main objectives: to foster dialogue and cooperation with former adversaries in the Warsaw Pact and to “manage” conflicts in areas on the European periphery, such as the Balkans. In keeping with the first objective, NATO established the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (1991; later replaced by the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council) to provide a forum for the exchange of views on political and security issues, as well as the enhance European security and stability through joint military training exercises with NATO and non-NATO states, including the former Soviet republics and allies. Special cooperative links were also set up with two PfP countries: Russia and Ukraine.
NATO in the former Yugoslavia and expansion into eastern Europe
The second objective entailed NATO’s first use of military force, when it entered the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995 by staging air strikes against Bosnian Serb positions around the capital city of Sarajevo. The subsequent Dayton Accords, which were initialed by representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, committed each state to respecting the others’ sovereignty and to settling disputes peacefully; it also laid the groundwork for stationing NATO peacekeeping troops in the region. A 60,000-strong Implementation Force (IFOR) was initially deployed, though a smaller contingent remained in Bosnia under a different name, the Stabilization Force (SFOR). In March 1999 NATO launched massive air strikes against Serbia in an attempt to force the Yugoslav government of Slobodan Milošević to accede to diplomatic provisions designed to protect the predominantly Muslim Albanian population in the province of Kosovo. Under the terms of a negotiated settlement to the fighting, NATO deployed a peacekeeping force called the Kosovo Force (KFOR).
The crisis over Kosovo and the ensuing war gave renewed impetus to efforts by the European Union (EU) to construct a new crisis-intervention force, which would make the EU less dependent on NATO and U.S. military resources for conflict management. These efforts prompted significant debates about whether enhancing the EU’s defensive capabilities would strengthen or weaken NATO. Simultaneously there was much discussion of the future of NATO in the post-Cold War era. Some observers argued that the alliance should be dissolved, noting that it was created to confront an enemy that no longer existed; others called for a broad expansion of NATO membership to include Russia. Most suggested alternative roles, including peacekeeping. By the start of the second decade of the 21st century, it appeared likely that the EU would not develop capabilities competitive with those of NATO or even seek to do so; as a result, earlier worries associated with the spectre of rivalry between the two Brussels-based organizations dissipated.
During the presidency of Bill Clinton (1993–2001), the United States led an initiative to enlarge NATO membership gradually to include some of the former Soviet allies. In the concurrent debate over enlargement, supporters of the initiative argued that NATO membership was the best way to begin the long process of integrating these states into regional political and economic institutions such as the EU. Some also feared future Russian aggression and suggested that NATO membership would guarantee freedom and security for the newly democratic regimes. Opponents pointed to the enormous cost of modernizing the military forces of new members; they also argued that enlargement, which Russia would regard as a provocation, would hinder democracy in that country and enhance the influence of hard-liners. Despite these disagreements, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland joined NATO in 1999; Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia were admitted in 2004 (these former Soviet and Warsaw Pact states later formed an extraordinary group known as the Bucharest Nine as a response to Russian aggression in the region). Albania and Croatia acceded to the alliance in 2009.
NATO relations with Russia in the post-September 11 world
Meanwhile, by the beginning of the 21st century, Russia and NATO had formed a strategic relationship. No longer considered NATO’s chief enemy, Russia cemented a new cooperative bond with NATO in 2001 to address such common concerns as international terrorism, nuclear nonproliferation, and arms control. This bond subsequently frayed, however, due to regional aggression by Russian Pres. Vladimir Putin. After Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, NATO strengthened ties with the latter country and established the NATO-Georgia Commission “to help Georgia achieve its goal of membership in NATO.” In 2014 pro-Russian Ukrainian Pres. Viktor Yanukovych fled months of popular protests, and Russia responded by invading the Ukrainian autonomous republic of Crimea. Russia illegally annexed Crimea and fomented uprisings in Ukraine’s Donbas region in an effort to reassert control over its neighbour. Ukraine checked the Russian-backed campaign in the Donbas, and NATO reaffirmed its support for Ukraine’s democratically elected government and its internationally recognized borders.
Events following the September 11 attacks in 2001 led to the forging of a new dynamic within the alliance, one that increasingly favoured the military engagement of members outside Europe, initially with a mission against Taliban forces in Afghanistan beginning in the summer of 2003 and subsequently with air operations against the regime of Muammar al-Qaddafi in Libya in early 2011. As a result of the increased tempo of military operations undertaken by the alliance, the long-standing issue of “burden sharing” was revived, with some officials warning that failure to share the costs of NATO operations more equitably would lead to unraveling of the alliance. At the time, however, most observers regarded that scenario as unlikely.
Later, the burden-sharing issue was raised once more by U.S. Pres. Donald Trump, who repeatedly criticized other NATO members for failing to devote a sufficient portion of their budgets to defense spending. Trump questioned the relevance of NATO and discussed withdrawing the United States from the alliance; even the suggestion of such an action was seen as a boon to Putin. However, Trump’s national security team moved to reassure allies that the U.S. remained committed to NATO, and, by the end of Trump’s term in 2021, the U.S. troop presence in Europe was almost entirely unchanged.
NATO and the Russian invasion of Ukraine
By the end of 2021, Russia had begun a massive military buildup along the Ukrainian frontier under the guise of joint maneuvers with the Belarusian army. In February 2022 there were as many as 190,000 Russian troops along the Russo-Ukrainian border, in Belarus, in Russian-occupied Crimea, and in the Russian-backed separatist enclave of Transdniestria in Moldova. On February 24 Putin announced the beginning of a “special military operation” and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Although the Russians made some early gains, their advances soon stalled against a spirited Ukrainian defense.
Ukrainian Pres. Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to Western countries for military aid, and individual NATO members began a massive transfer of hardware to bolster the Ukrainian arsenal. The administration of U.S. Pres. Joe Biden took a leading role in marshaling the response to the greatest threat to European security since World War II. The speed and unity of NATO’s reaction to Russian aggression in Ukraine dramatically dispelled any doubts about the continued relevance of the alliance.
Sweden and Finland, two countries with a long history of neutrality, announced their intention to join NATO in the wake of the Russian invasion, and the U.S. deployed additional military assets to Poland and the Baltic states. In June 2022, at the first annual NATO summit since the invasion, NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg announced “the biggest overhaul of our collectivedeterrence and defense since the Cold War.” In addition to formally inviting Sweden and Finland to join the alliance, Stoltenberg declared that NATO’s rapid reaction force, a collection of air, sea, and land units maintained at a state of high readiness, would increase from 40,000 troops to more than 300,000. In April 2023 Finland became the 31st member of NATO, but Sweden’s accession was held up by objections from Turkey and Hungary until March 2024, when Sweden became the alliance’s 32nd member.

October 15, 2026 | 03:19 pm
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - China and North Korea on Thursday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aimed at rejuvenating trade and commerce after years of strained ties and disruptions.
A ceremony was held to launch the New Yalu River Bridge, Chinese state media Xinhua News reported.
Meanwhile, China News Service showed visuals of trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea on the bridge, which itself was decorated in flags.
Spectators crowded on a road on the Chinese side, in Dandong city, overlooking the ceremony. In Sinuiju city on the North Korean side, work on the approaching road and compound remained unfinished.
'A new chapter'
The cable-stayed bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused until now due to lack of connecting roads on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap News agency reported.
The opening was further delayed by the COVID pandemic which prompted North Korea to close its borders. Train journeys between the East Asian neighbors only restarted in March after six years, but Pyongyang is yet to resume issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, which once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
The bridge's opening marks the latest sign of warning ties between Beijing and Pyongyang which have conducted two summits between their leaders in the past year.
"(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency said.
He added that the border crossing would "strongly promote" economic and trade cooperation and strengthen exchanges between their people.
A conduit for trade
Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told the AFP news agency he expected hundreds of vehicles to cross every day.
"The bridge could become a conduit for China's abundant goods and resources to flow into North Korea and give its economy a significant boost," he said.
At the same time, experts believe North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.
"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies. But it will help move heavy equipment and raw material North Korea needs for development, he said.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner despite a series of UN sanctions banning the flow of goods and workers to North Korea over its missile and nuclear weapons program.

Can India's latest FTAs put it on the road to Viksit Atmanirbhar Bharat?
India's FTAs can boost export-led growth, but sustainable gains will depend on responsible subsidies, stronger labour standards and environment-friendly production
premium
A cargo ship at port highlights India’s growing role in global trade and its push to expand export markets through free trade agreements
India, a country known to have been reticent in liberalising trade till very recently, has negotiated around nine agreements between 2021 and 2026. The free trade agreement (FTA) partners span around 38 developed countries and, as per latest reports, India is negotiating with eight to nine blocs and individual countries to collectively account for 75 per cent of global trade.
For a country branded a “tariff king” by US President Donald Trump, and perceived as obstructionist at the World Trade Organization, India seems to be redrawing its earlier perceptions in the world over the last 5 years.
India’s recent surge in signing FTAs seems to be the result of a number of developments. Tackling China in competition in domestic markets is near-impossible (despite lower labour costs) without increasing sales volumes in the markets abroad which, in turn, help build scale economies, reducing production costs. Additionally, the recent Trump tariffs, broadly impacting all economies of the world, have pushed most countries to reach trade deals at an unprecedented rate, reflecting a collective commitment to free trade.
Indian FTAs span countries which are developed markets, including the European Union (EU), European Free Trade Association (Efta), and Australia, as well as countries which are home to a significant portion of the Indian diaspora. These include the United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates and Oman. Finally, negotiations are in progress with countries which would help secure India’s supply chain of critical rare earth elements. Peru and Chile fall under this category. India’s earlier comprehensive agreements with Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia have their own role in comprehensive cooperation on multiple fronts. The India-EU trade deal, branded as the “mother of all trade deals”, is creating a positive outlook for future growth in external demand-driven economic growth. However, do the FTAs have implications for India’s vision of becoming atmanirbhar and, finally, viksit?
In a world where the US turns protectionist and large corporates strategise, keeping tensions with China in mind, the FTAs provide an opportunity for Indian businesses and the Indian government to prioritise some changes and avoid some others to enable longer term sustainability of India’s position in global markets as well as catapult India to a Viksit Bharat.
A quick look at the pain points for globalisation, emerging from the stalemate at the WTO, the experience of mega-regional agreements, and current reactions from the US could help draw some quick lessons on how India could use this opportunity to make the best of the world’s China+1 strategy.
Production subsidies and dumping
In the last couple of decades, one observes the repeated use of anti-dumping cases against countries like China at the WTO. State-sponsored unfair subsidies in China helped reap cost advantages beyond the scale economies of operations. Most Chinese products thus got cheaper than those of China’s counterparts across the world. While the Chinese labour costs were lower, the greater scale of operations, further facilitated by state subsidies on a massive scale, have adversely impacted most countries, especially the developed West. Advantages in production costs due to lower labour costs should be fair, providing some breathing space for production by other countries. While India prioritises growth through production linked incentives (PLIs), a sunset clause linked to growth in the scale of operations or transitioning to research and development (R&D)-linked subsidies is ideal for sustained export-led growth.
Environment
The developed world is concerned about environmental standards and protection of marine life. The WTO agreement on fisheries subsidies, reached in 2022, and the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) of the EU are worth our attention. The EU tries to protect the environment and tax non-environment-friendly methods of production. The India-EU FTA does not make any carve-outs on the applicability of the CBAM. In essence, India faces the TBT (technical barriers to trade) on similar levels as other countries. Adoption of environment-friendly production techniques by Indian businesses would help both in achieving greater market access in any developed country and in moving towards a truly Viksit Bharat.
Forced labour
The US has imposed additional tariffs for the use of forced labour or labour-unfriendly work conditions against selected countries, including India through the forced-labour Section 301 tariffs. These tariffs are a result of the US’s failure to block labour-unfriendly products entering the US markets from countries like China. Going back to 2013, India’s use of child labour for manufacturing rugby balls for Summit Sports in Australia drew enough negative media attention internationally. While the WTO has never acted to ensure quality work standards for workers involved in producing tradable goods, the International Labour Organization (ILO) standards would be ideal. Once again moving towards viable labour standards, including appropriate overtime pay, would create the base for a Viksit Bharat and avoid future possibilities of tariffs on grounds of forced labour.
Tariff-jumping transhipment
Rules of origin violations (to bypass tariffs) have been highlighted by the US recently. India earlier raised similar issues with regard to China, leading to a review of the India-Asean (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) agreement. Contrary to China’s conditions, India signing FTAs with most countries would allow it market access at lower tariff rates and the need to bypass tariffs should not arise. India should avoid using FTAs to push its products to non-FTA countries.
It may be prudent to note that mega-regional agreements like the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) have very different stands on each of the four areas mentioned above. While the CPTPP commits to environment-friendly production, protection of labour standards and avoiding state-sponsored production subsidies, the China-led RCEP is nearly silent on all of these. It is easy to see that relaxed labour and environment standards along with state subsidies are the building blocks of sustained trade advantage for nations like China and Vietnam. The developed West sees these as unfair to their own workers/citizens as jobs are lost along with environmental degradation in exchange for cheaper imported products.
Learning from the above, India has the choice to: a) craft its subsidies with appropriate sunset clauses, b) protect labour standards, and c) adopt environment-friendly production to sustainably position itself in global markets. This would be the basis of a truly Viksit Bharat.
The writer is associate professor of economics at the Indian Institutes of Management (IIM) Nagpur

high_priority_articles.title: IPS calls for investment- and export-led growth to sustain Sri Lanka’s recovery - Hiru News
high_priority_articles.summary: IPS calls for investment- and export-led growth to sustain Sri Lanka’s recovery  Hiru News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Sri Lanka must move away from debt-financed spending, tax concessions and import-intensive consumption to sustain its economic recovery, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) has said, calling for a growth strategy centred on private investment, productivity and competitive exports.
In its newly released Sri Lanka: State of the Economy 2026 report, titled Policy Choices for Durable Growth, the IPS said the country’s next challenge was to accelerate economic growth without reopening the fiscal and external vulnerabilities that contributed to the 2022 economic crisis.
With limited fiscal and external space, the next phase of expansion must depend on stronger investment, a more competitive and diversified export sector, and the creation of better-quality jobs, the institute said.
“Sri Lanka can no longer rely on debt-financed spending, tax concessions or import-intensive consumption as drivers of growth,” the IPS said in a statement announcing the report.
The assessment comes as the economy continues to recover from the crisis. Real GDP grew by 5% in both 2024 and 2025, and by 4.7% in the first half of 2026, according to the release.
Inflation has eased considerably from its 2022 peak, progress has been made in external debt restructuring, and foreign reserves have been rebuilt to more comfortable levels, the institute said.
However, sustaining these gains will require a growth model that can withstand future shocks while delivering broad-based improvements in living standards.
The report calls for continued macroeconomic stability alongside measures to improve productivity and ensure more effective use of scarce public resources.
“The challenge then is to accelerate growth without reopening the fiscal and external vulnerabilities that contributed to the crisis,” the release said.
Human capital development and labour market reforms are also identified as central to the next phase of growth. The IPS highlighted the need to address skills gaps, create better-quality employment and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
With around two-thirds of Sri Lanka’s workers employed informally, the report identifies improved labour market outcomes and stronger social protection as priorities for ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are more widely shared.
The institute said better-quality employment and a workforce equipped with relevant skills would be essential to improving productivity and enabling more people to participate in and benefit from economic expansion.
Building resilience to climate-related disruptions, energy shocks and external pressures is another key requirement for sustained economic progress.
Recent climate-related disruptions and global energy shocks have demonstrated the importance of placing resilience at the centre of Sri Lanka’s development strategy, the IPS said.
Investment in renewable energy, food systems, infrastructure and disaster preparedness could help protect future growth while reducing the economy’s exposure to shocks.
The report also examines how infrastructure investment, regional development and responses to changing population dynamics could contribute to more inclusive growth.
Its policy recommendations cover trade, fiscal management, labour markets, urbanisation, energy, agriculture, social protection and human capital development.
The IPS said Sri Lanka could achieve its long-term development ambitions through reforms that strengthen competitiveness and resilience while ensuring the benefits of economic progress are broadly shared.

Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq may get access to new trade routes connecting Europe, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia after an agreement between Port of NEOM and CEVA Almajdouie Logistics to investigate integrated cargo services linking the Red Sea with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations and Iraq.
The planned logistical corridor comes as the region’s war worsens and shipping via the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, making other trade routes more important for Iraq and other Gulf nations.
Under a memorandum of understanding, the two corporations will look into methods to optimize the flow of products along the Europe-Egypt-Saudi Arabia-GCC-Iraq corridor by integrating marine shipping with land transport, customs clearing, storage, and cross-border distribution.
The Port of NEOM, situated in Saudi Arabia’s northwestern Red Sea area, is being developed as a logistics hub linking international shipping lines to domestic markets.
The cooperation would use the port’s marine links and CEVA Almajdouie Logistics’ regional transport network to provide companies with better coordinated cargo services between ports and ultimate destinations.
For Iraq, the corridor might offer an extra route for imports and commercial cargo coming from Europe and other foreign markets, thus decreasing dependence on regular Gulf shipping routes.
The effort also emphasizes Saudi Arabia’s expanding importance in linking Iraq to regional and worldwide supply chains, especially as corporations seek alternatives to sea routes vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions.
The company seek to study combined customer service, market growth, and logistical solutions for various sorts of cargo.
The arrangement is still exploratory, with no precise investment value, implementation timeline, or verified cargo quantities stated.
While the planned corridor has the potential to increase Iraq’s economic relations with Saudi Arabia and other GCC nations, its actual effects will be determined by the development of cross-border transportation services, customs procedures, and business demand.

high_priority_articles.title: Tings Chak: How Brazil’s election could reshape relations with China - Friends of Socialist China
high_priority_articles.summary: Tings Chak: How Brazil’s election could reshape relations with China  Friends of Socialist China
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The following article by Tings Chak, Asia Co-Coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and an editor of the international edition of Wenhua Zongheng: A Journal of Contemporary Chinese Thought, examines what is at stake for China-Brazil relations in Brazil’s presidential runoff on October 25 between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.
Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that “has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South”. Under Lula, this cooperation has extended to industrial development, infrastructure, science and technology – and to Brazil’s popular movements, with the Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) working with Chinese institutions on agricultural mechanisation, bioinputs and AI tools for agroecology built on Chinese open-source models.
Flávio Bolsonaro, by contrast, has offered Brazil to Washington as the “solution” to its dependence on China for critical minerals, and his campaign has proposed preventing Brazil’s Pix payment system from connecting to non-Western networks. With the Trump administration proclaiming a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, Brazil – Latin America’s largest economy and a founding member of BRICS – has become “a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region”.
Tings notes that Chinese analysts anticipate “cold politics, hot economics” under a Flávio presidency, with commodity trade continuing but strategic cooperation deteriorating, as it did under his father. She concludes that the future of China-Brazil cooperation “will depend on the capacity of organised popular forces to build a sovereign national project and turn international cooperation into lasting changes in people’s lives”.
This article first appeared in BreakThrough News.
On October 25, Brazilians will return to the polls to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in an attempted coup. The first round gave Flávio 47% of valid votes against Lula’s 45%, revealing the enduring strength of the far right four years after its electoral defeat. The runoff takes place as Donald Trump seeks to restore US domination over Latin America, with Brazil emerging as a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region.
Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South. Under Lula and Xi Jinping, this relationship has deepened through cooperation in industrial development, infrastructure, science, and technology. The election will determine whether this project advances or Brazil’s international orientation is subordinated to Washington’s renewed Monroe Doctrine as part of the continent’s rightward shift.
Since Lula’s return to the presidency in 2023, the two governments have connected Chinese cooperation with Brazil’s development programs, including Nova Indústria Brasil, the Growth Acceleration Program (PAC), and the Ecological Transformation Plan. Lula’s May 2025 visit to Beijing produced 36 agreements covering infrastructure, finance, artificial intelligence, public health, and industrial cooperation. Behind these agreements is a long-standing challenge: overcoming Brazil’s dependent position in the international division of labor, where commodity exports continue to outweigh advanced industrial and technological development.
This cooperation has also reached Brazilian popular movements. Through the International Association for Popular Cooperation (Baobab), Brazil’s Landless Rural Workers’ Movement (MST) and other organizations have worked with Chinese institutions on agricultural mechanization, bioinputs, and digital technologies for family farming. These initiatives include the Digital Family Farming and Agroecology Laboratory and IARAA, an artificial intelligence project for agroecology and agrarian reform developed by Brazilian popular movements using Chinese open-source models. In a countryside marked by extreme concentrations of land, machinery, and capital, such cooperation offers new tools to peasant organizations fighting for agrarian reform and the production of healthy food.
Brazil’s relationship with China also reveals the different class interests at work in the country, with contradictions particularly visible in the countryside. Massive exports of soybeans, meat, and minerals have continued under both Bolsonaro and Lula, but their governments have pursued very different political relationships with Beijing. While Jair Bolsonaro attacked China and aligned himself with Washington, Lula has sought to deepen strategic cooperation, including in industrial development, technology, and agrarian reform. Flávio Bolsonaro now promises an “economically pragmatic” relationship with China while cultivating close ties with Trump. For sectors of Brazil’s ruling classes that profit from commodity exports, continuing to sell to China while embracing Washington’s political agenda presents little contradiction. For Brazil’s efforts to rebuild its industry and develop technological sovereignty, the consequences are far greater.
The return of the Monroe Doctrine
Washington’s ambitions were made explicit in its November 2025 National Security Strategy, which announced a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, seeking to restore US pre-eminence in the Western Hemisphere and deny outside powers control over strategic resources and infrastructure. Five days later, China published its third Latin America policy paper, reaffirming sovereignty, non-interference, regional integration, technological cooperation, and support for the region as a Zone of Peace. The two documents reveal fundamentally different approaches to the political future of the continent.
Brazil’s position is decisive. As Latin America’s largest economy, a founding BRICS member, and a leading participant in Mercosur, it possesses industrial, scientific, and political capacities that could strengthen independent development across Latin America and beyond.
The emergence of a new technological era makes this struggle particularly consequential. Brazil is among the few countries of the Global South capable of pursuing digital and technological sovereignty that could benefit its neighbors and parts of Africa. Its roughly 23% share of global rare earth reserves is an important starting point, but control over minerals alone is insufficient. The greater challenge is developing the capacity to process them, manufacture advanced components, and build the digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence systems, and technologies that will shape future production.
Flávio has made his orientation clear. Speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in the United States in March 2026, he offered Brazil as the “solution” to Washington’s dependence on China for critical minerals, explicitly linking rare earths to artificial intelligence and US military superiority. Chinese economic reporting has also described proposals from his team to exclude China from rare-earth supply chains. Rather than using Brazil’s resources to develop its own industrial and technological capacities, this agenda would place them at the service of US technological and military power.
The same political orientation extends to digital sovereignty. In July 2026, Flávio’s campaign submitted proposals to US trade authorities that included preventing Brazil’s Pix payment system from connecting to non-Western international payment networks and loosening commitments within Mercosur. These proposals converge with a wider US campaign involving tariffs, digital regulation, strategic minerals, and attempts to influence Brazil’s electoral process. Meanwhile, Washington’s January 2026 bombing on Venezuela and kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores demonstrated how far it is prepared to go to impose its will on the continent.
BRICS and the struggle for an independent foreign policy
Brazil, particularly under Lula, has helped build institutions through which countries of the Global South can reduce their dependence on Western-dominated structures. At the July 2025 BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, the group advanced cooperation on development finance, local-currency transactions, and international institutional reform. The New Development Bank, headed by former Brazilian president Dilma Rousseff, is an important expression of this effort.
The BRICS cannot automatically overcome economic dependency or guarantee sovereignty for working people. Yet its expansion offers greater room for independent development, provided that participating governments have the political commitment to use these possibilities.
Brazil’s history reveals how difficult that independence has been to defend. In 1961, vice-president João Goulart became the first high-ranking representative of a Latin American government to visit the People’s Republic of China, meeting Mao Zedong when revolutionary China remained diplomatically isolated and subjected to US sanctions. Three years later, Goulart was overthrown in a US-backed civil-military coup that inaugurated a 21-year dictatorship. The early history of China–Brazil friendship was inseparable from struggles over national sovereignty, agrarian reform, and the forces determined to suppress them.
The international material conditions for South–South cooperation are considerably more favorable today, but political direction remains decisive. Jair Bolsonaro hosted the 2019 BRICS summit in Brasília while pursuing close alignment with Washington. A government can weaken institutions from within by abandoning the commitments that give them political substance.
The far right’s resurgence also reflects the enduring power of Brazil’s own ruling classes. B

high_priority_articles.title: Africa’s 20 Largest Economies in 2026: South Africa Leads, Kenya Rises, Tanzania Slips - Uchumi360
high_priority_articles.summary: Africa’s 20 Largest Economies in 2026: South Africa Leads, Kenya Rises, Tanzania Slips  Uchumi360
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Ready
South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy at about US$489 billion in 2026, but the continent’s economic hierarchy is shifting rapidly as Kenya, Ghana, Ethiopia, DRC and Côte d’Ivoire gain scale. Tanzania ranks 12th while Uganda continues to close the gap.
Africa’s economic hierarchy is changing faster than the familiar rankings of the past would suggest. South Africa remains the continent’s largest economy in nominal terms at an estimated US$489.08 billion in 2026, followed by Egypt at US$442.89 billion and Nigeria at US$386.67 billion. But beyond the top three, a more consequential reshuffling is taking place. Kenya has consolidated its position as East Africa’s largest economy at US$151.15 billion, Ghana has climbed to eighth, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo have both crossed US$120 billion, Côte d’Ivoire has moved above Tanzania, and Uganda is now approaching the US$75 billion threshold.
The ranking, based on the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook framework and the country figures supplied for 2026, captures more than economic size. It reflects the combined effect of real growth, inflation, exchange rates, commodity cycles, demographic expansion and revisions to national accounts. The IMF’s October WEO confirms that the database covers GDP, inflation, trade and other macroeconomic indicators, with projections extending several years ahead.
That distinction matters because nominal GDP measured in US dollars can move sharply even when the underlying economy changes more gradually. A country can grow strongly in real terms but slip in the ranking if its currency depreciates heavily against the dollar. Another can move rapidly upward because of higher commodity revenues, currency appreciation or rebasing. The ranking therefore provides a useful picture of economic scale, but not a complete measure of living standards, productivity or development.
South Africa Holds The Top Position, But Its Growth Remains Weak
South Africa’s estimated US$489.08 billion economy keeps it comfortably at the top of the African ranking, ahead of Egypt and Nigeria. Yet the size of the economy contrasts with weak real expansion. The IMF expects South Africa to grow by only about 1 percent in 2026, making it one of the slowest growing economies among Africa’s top 20.
That creates a familiar South African paradox. The country retains the continent’s deepest financial markets, largest industrial base, sophisticated corporate sector and major mining industry, but growth remains constrained by infrastructure weaknesses, power supply challenges, logistics bottlenecks, unemployment and low investment.
South Africa remains number one because of the scale accumulated over decades. The more important question is how long it can preserve that position if its growth remains close to 1 percent while several economies further down the ranking expand at 5 percent, 6 percent or more.
Egypt, at US$442.89 billion, is much closer. The IMF projects Egypt’s real GDP growth at about 5.1 percent in 2026, meaning the gap between Africa’s first and second largest economies can narrow significantly if Egypt sustains stronger expansion and stabilises its currency.
Nigeria Is Still Enormous, But No Longer Africa’s Unchallenged Giant
Nigeria’s position at US$386.67 billion marks a striking reversal from the years when it regularly appeared as Africa’s largest economy.
The country remains the continent’s most populous market and one of its largest oil producers, but currency depreciation has dramatically changed its nominal GDP position in US dollars. The naira’s weakening has reduced the dollar value of domestic output, even when measured economic activity has continued growing in local terms.
The IMF projects Nigeria’s real GDP growth at about 4.2 percent in 2026. That is stronger than South Africa’s, but still below the pace being recorded by several emerging African economies.
Nigeria therefore demonstrates one of the central weaknesses of nominal GDP rankings. Economic size in dollars depends partly on what happens in foreign exchange markets. A country can remain economically significant, add millions of consumers and increase production while falling down the ranking because its currency loses value.
The result is that Africa’s largest population no longer automatically produces Africa’s largest nominal economy.
North Africa Still Controls A Large Share Of The Top Five
North Africa remains heavily represented near the top. Egypt ranks second, Algeria fourth at US$331.89 billion and Morocco fifth at US$195.63 billion.
Algeria’s position remains closely connected to hydrocarbons, with oil and gas revenues continuing to support export earnings, government finances and the broader economy. The IMF expects growth of about 3.8 percent in 2026.
Morocco’s US$195.63 billion economy is almost US$40 billion larger than Angola’s and more than twice Tanzania’s. Unlike several commodity dominated economies, Morocco has gradually built a wider production base across automotive manufacturing, aerospace components, tourism, phosphates, agriculture, logistics and increasingly renewable energy and industrial exports. The IMF projects Moroccan growth at roughly 4.5 percent in 2026.
The broader lesson is that nominal scale is increasingly being determined not only by resource endowment, but by whether countries can build diversified sectors capable of generating exports, domestic value addition and stable foreign exchange earnings.
Angola Has Rebuilt Its Position Through Oil, But Diversification Remains The Test
Angola ranks sixth at US$157.30 billion, ahead of Kenya. Its economic position remains heavily linked to oil, which continues to dominate export earnings and public revenue. The IMF expects Angola to grow around 4.4 percent in 2026. That growth gives Angola room to consolidate its position, but the structure of the economy remains a vulnerability. Oil can push GDP upward quickly when prices and production are favourable, but it also exposes the country to sharp external shocks when global markets turn.
Angola’s ranking therefore says more about economic scale than diversification. The long term challenge remains converting hydrocarbon wealth into manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, services and industries capable of sustaining growth after oil’s relative importance declines.
Kenya Has Become East Africa’s Clear Economic Leader
Kenya’s rise to seventh place at US$151.15 billion is one of the most significant shifts in Africa’s economic ranking.
The country now stands more than US$55 billion ahead of Tanzania and almost US$79 billion above Uganda. Kenya has built its scale through a relatively diversified economic base that includes financial services, telecommunications, transport, agriculture, tourism, real estate, professional services, manufacturing and a large regional corporate sector. Its growth is not the fastest in East Africa. The IMF expects Kenya to expand by about 4.5 percent in 2026, compared with 9.2 percent for Ethiopia, 6 percent for Tanzania and 6.2 percent for Uganda.
Kenya’s advantage is the stock of economic activity already accumulated. Nairobi has become a regional headquarters for banks, technology companies, professional firms, development institutions and multinational corporations. Its financial system is deeper than most regional peers, while the country has also built strong export sectors in horticulture, tea, tourism and business services.
The ranking also shows why East Africa is becoming a larger part of Africa’s overall economic story. Kenya, Ethiopia, DRC, Tanzania and Uganda all feature within the continent’s top 13 economies.
Ghana’s US$128.64 Billion Economy Is One Of The Ranking’s Biggest Stories
Ghana’s rise to eighth place at US$128.64 billion places it ahead of Ethiopia, DRC, Côte d’Ivoire and Tanzania. That is significant because Ghana has only a fraction of the population of Ethiopia or Tanzania. Its ranking reflects the recovery of the economy, currency movements, commodity exports and the size of its services and extractive sectors. The IMF projects Ghana to grow about 5.7 percent in 2026.
Ghana’s position also illustrates how quickly African rankings can change after periods of currency and debt instability. A stronger cedi, lower inflation, fiscal adjustment and recovery in domestic activity can substantially increase the dollar value of the economy even before structural changes are fully visible. For this reason, Ghana’s eighth place should be watched over several years before being interpreted as a permanent new equilibrium.
Ethiopia Is Growing Faster Than Almost Every Major African Economy
Ethiopia ranks ninth at US$127.15 billion, but its growth rate makes it one of the most consequential economies in the ranking. The IMF expects Ethiopia’s real economy to expand by about 9.2 percent in 2026, the fastest rate among the continent’s major economies listed here.
If sustained, that pace can dramatically change the ranking over time. At 9 percent annual real growth, an economy roughly doubles in size in about eight years before considering inflation and exchange rate effects.
Ethiopia’s challenge is that extremely rapid domestic growth has existed alongside significant foreign exchange shortages, inflation, external debt pressures and a major currency adjustment. Those factors can suppress nominal GDP in US dollar terms even when local production is expanding rapidly.
The country therefore illustrates the opposite side of the Nigerian problem. Ethiopia can be one of Africa’s fastest growing economies without immediately becoming one of the largest in dollar terms because currency effects reduce the international value of domestic output.
DRC Is Turning Mineral Wealth Into Economic Scale
The Democratic Republic of Congo ranks tenth at US$122.28 billion. Its ascent is closely tied to mining, particularly copper and cobalt, which have become increasingly strategic to global supply chains linke

high_priority_articles.title: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic Opportunity, Economic Imperative or Geopolitical Gamble? - Business & Financial Times
high_priority_articles.summary: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic Opportunity, Economic Imperative or Geopolitical Gamble?  Business & Financial Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Hon. Samuel Okudzeto Abalakwa, Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister, announced cabinet’s approval for Ghana’s application to join the BRICS, at a joint press briefing with India’s External Affairs Minister during his visit to Accra. The Honourable Minister linked the decision to the President’s “New Economy” agenda and the desire for Ghana to chart its own path without being constrained by the conditionalities of a few international institutions. This announcement formalises a relationship that trade data has been describing for years.
The open questions are what formal membership adds, what it might cost, and how businesses should position themselves while the process plays out. The conversation is more relevant now, as Ghana transitions from a period of macroeconomic stabilisation towards one focused on investment-led growth and structural transformation.
Understanding BRICS and Why It Matters
What began in the early 2000s as an economic acronym coined to describe the fast-growing emerging economies of Brazil, Russia, India and China has evolved into one of the most influential geopolitical and economic blocs in the world. South Africa joined the grouping in 2010, transforming BRIC into BRICS and providing Africa with representation within the bloc. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE later joined, followed by Indonesia in 2025, bringing membership to 11, with Nigeria and several other countries holding partner status.
The group’s main institution is the New Development Bank (NDB), headquartered in Shanghai. The bank has approved over 120 projects worth about US$40 billion and admits new members on the condition that the founding BRICS countries' capital share never falls below 55%. One stated ambition - reducing reliance on the US Dollar - remains a key aspiration yet to be realised.
BRICS today is no longer simply a forum for emerging economies. It represents a broader vision for increasing the influence of developing nations within global governance structures. For many countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America, the appeal of BRICS lies not in replacing existing global institutions, but in creating additional options. In an increasingly uncertain global environment characterised by economic fragmentation, geopolitical competition and shifting trade dynamics, diversification has become a strategic necessity.
Why Ghana Is Looking Towards BRICS
Ghana's interest in BRICS comes at a pivotal moment in its economic journey.
Following years of economic turbulence, debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms, the Country has made notable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability. Economic discussions are increasingly shifting from stabilisation towards growth, productivity, investment and industrialisation. Internal economic briefings and policy discussions increasingly focus on how Ghana can move from recovery to sustainable private-sector-led growth.
At the same time, the global economic environment is changing. Emerging markets are playing a larger role in global trade and investment flows, while developing countries are seeking greater influence within international institutions.
Against this backdrop, BRICS presents Ghana with an opportunity to expand its economic options.
Government officials have publicly framed the proposed membership as part of a broader strategy to diversify international partnerships and create new avenues for cooperation. This rationale aligns closely with the Country's broader ambitions around industrialisation, infrastructure development, job creation and economic transformation.
The Economic Case for Membership
The strongest arguments in favour of Ghana joining BRICS are arguably economic rather than political. Four key areas of potential benefit to Ghana have been highlighted below:
· Alignment with where Ghana's trade already goes: This is the strongest economic argument. In 2025, the UAE took 25.9% of Ghana's exports, India 16.0%, South Africa 10.3% and China 4.9%. All four are BRICS members, which means roughly 57% of Ghana's export earnings already flow to the bloc. On the import side, China remained Ghana's largest supplier at about 23% of imports in the fourth quarter of 2025. Membership could institutionalise relationships that are already central to Ghana's balance of payments, while opening additional channels for exports and investment promotion.
· Development financing options: Ghana has completed a demanding IMF programme and now engages the Fund through a Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI), a non-financing arrangement that offers technical support and policy guidance. With no IMF money on the table, access to the NDB for infrastructure financing (energy, rail, water, digital) would widen the menu of long-tenor capital at a time when Ghana needs to finance growth. These investments will be essential if the Country is to realise its ambition of becoming a competitive industrial economy.
· Industrial and technology partnerships: The visit by India’s External Affairs Minister itself showed what is on offer, with plans announced to deepen cooperation in railways, pharmaceuticals, ICT, defence, agriculture and science and technology. If Ghana uses membership to negotiate local value addition, such as gold refining, cocoa processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing, rather than simply more raw commodity exports, the growth dividend could be real.
· Negotiating leverage: Being in more rooms strengthens Ghana's hand with every partner, including the Bretton Woods institutions, on debt treatment, climate finance and conditionality, amongst others.
Lessons from Africa's BRICS Experience
To understand what BRICS membership could mean for Ghana, it is important to examine the experiences of African countries already within the bloc.
South Africa's journey offers perhaps the most relevant case study. Since joining BRICS in 2010, South Africa has used the platform to deepen trade and investment relationships, expand diplomatic influence and access development financing through the New Development Bank. The NDB's first South African loan in 2016 supported renewable energy, and the bank has since backed 13 projects there worth around US$9 billion (in current terms), including a loan of up to US$1 billion for water and sanitation infrastructure under the Municipal Infrastructure Grant programme. The lesson is that the NDB can be a meaningful infrastructure financier for a member with a strong project pipeline and capable state entities. The Country continues to benefit from this association, while simultaneously maintaining strong economic relationships with Europe and the United States.
Ethiopia, which joined in 2024, presents a cautionary story. At admission, one Ethiopian economist judged that the direct economic benefit would be modest, but that membership would improve investor perception and widen options for development finance. Ethiopian analysts have observed that the country's trade and investment ties are stronger with individual BRICS countries such as China, Saudi Arabia and India than with the bloc as a whole, and that membership has not offset the AGOA benefits and Western privileges that were lost. The Ethiopian Economics Association also warned that trading in local currencies could worsen forex constraints and complicate Dollar-based trade with other partners, recommending that Ethiopia manages it relationship with both BRICS and the West in the short run to the benefit of the country.
Perhaps the most important lesson from these experiences is that BRICS membership itself does not create economic transformation. Membership rewards countries that come with bankable projects and strong institutions, and it does not by itself replace Western market access. South Africa's gains did not emerge simply because it joined BRICS; they emerged because the country actively leveraged membership to attract investment, strengthen trade relationships and promote national economic priorities.
The challenges and considerations
While the economic opportunities are compelling, it would be naïve to assume that BRICS membership comes without risks.
· Western Economic Relationships management is an immediate risk: The European Union, United States and United Kingdom remain among Ghana's most important development partners, export destinations and sources of foreign direct investment.
