high_priority_articles.summary: Nigeria to address red tape affecting digital trade under AfCFTA  The Guardian Nigeria News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Nigeria is working with the World Bank Group to identify gaps in its digital trade regulations as it seeks to align a pending digital economy bill and a planned e-commerce policy with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Protocol on Digital Trade.
The regulatory gap analysis is part of efforts to ensure that the protocol, its annexes and Nigeria’s domestic laws and policies work together, according to the National Coordinator and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian AfCFTA Coordination Office (NACO), Patience Okala.
Okala said Nigerian businesses had identified Ghana, Egypt, Rwanda, South Africa and Kenya as priority markets for expansion and regulators from the five countries were brought to Lagos to examine market-access requirements and identify areas where their processes could be aligned or mutually recognised.
Okala said the challenge, however, extends beyond aligning regulations. Businesses, she said, need reliable ways to verify trading partners, make and receive payments, transfer data securely and use digital systems that work across national borders.
She said Nigeria was one of three pilot countries selected for the Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade (ADAPT) initiative, run by the AfCFTA Secretariat and the Tony Blair Institute, alongside Egypt and Kenya. A team had been inaugurated in Nigeria to work on the initiative, which is intended to advance interoperability between digital systems and provide a basis for implementing the protocol.
Citing World Trade Organisation records, she said African exports of digitally delivered services grew by 15 per cent in 2024, which she described as the fastest growth recorded in any region. She said this growth underscored the need for appropriate regulatory arrangements, adding that the protocol’s provisions and annexes need to align with Nigeria’s existing regulatory framework for it to be fully implemented.
Chief Executive Officer, Better Than Cash Alliance, Nshuti Mbabazi, said the implementation of the protocol must move beyond written agreements to practical testing of cross-border payment arrangements.
Responding to a question about how a Nigerian seller could receive payment for goods ordered from Kenya, Mbabazi said the framework must be tested through actual transactions to identify the barriers preventing businesses from completing payments reliably. She proposed identifying a small group of traders willing to buy and sell along the Nigeria–East Africa corridor and using their transactions to test the framework. The exercise, she said, would help establish the actual obstacles to trusted electronic payments.
She said the Better Than Cash Alliance would work to activate cross-border digital trade payment proofs of concept, adding that similar work had started in East Africa and could also be undertaken between Nigeria and East African markets.
According to her, businesses should be able to access information required to register and verify their operations online without physically visiting offices. She added that trusted digital identity recognised across participating African markets would help businesses establish legitimacy and build confidence among prospective trading partners.
Drawing on her experience in Aba’s textiles, leather and manufacturing sectors, Mbabazi said digital platforms have made communication with potential customers easier, but challenges persist when businesses need to make payments or move goods across borders as affordable payment arrangements and reliable ways to track goods until delivery is needed.
Mbabazi highlighted the potential of fintech passporting, under which a company licensed in Nigeria could expand into another participating African country without repeating extensive regulatory procedures. She urged African countries to work across regional economic communities, including the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the East African Community (EAC), to establish interoperable systems that make cross-border transactions as straightforward as domestic ones.
Head of Regulatory Unit at the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), Ibukunoluwa Owa, said secure cross-border data transfers were essential to building trust among businesses trading under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), urging Nigerian operators to understand and comply with the country’s data protection requirements before expanding into other African markets. She outlined different mechanisms for obtaining approval, including an adequacy route under which the commission assesses whether a destination country provides comparable protection.
Owa identified standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, certification mechanisms and codes of conduct as possible instruments for cross-border data transfers, subject to applicable requirements. She explained that contractual clauses could be adapted to specific transactions, while binding corporate rules could support transfers within groups of companies operating in different countries.
Owa said limited exceptions, including informed consent and contractual necessity, could apply in specific circumstances. However, she advised businesses that transferred data regularly to rely on adequacy decisions or transfer instruments rather than treating these exceptions as their principal route.
She identified digital identity, secure data transfers and regulatory convergence as important to building trust in cross-border digital trade. She said Nigeria was leading a regulatory harmonisation working group under the Network of Africa Data Protection Authorities to improve alignment of cross-border data transfer rules and make compliance easier for businesses operating across jurisdictions.
Representing the Director of e-governance services at the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Oluwatosin Lewis-Okoh, said digital trade required reliable broadband, interoperable systems and trusted identities, alongside payment and customs arrangements that supported transactions from identifying buyers and sellers to exchanging data, settling payments and processing customs documentation.
On digital identity and trust, she said businesses trading across borders need reliable ways to establish the identities of the people and organisations they trade with. She referred to changes involving public key infrastructure and the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), explaining that trusted identity systems are key to establishing confidence between buyers and sellers in different countries.
She illustrated this with the example of a Nigerian fashion entrepreneur selling to a customer in Kigali. 
For the transaction to succeed, the seller would need a verified customer identity, a payment arrangement that could settle across borders, electronic customs documentation and assurance that the customer’s personal data was protected. “If one of these links breaks, the sale breaks,” she said, stressing the need for integrated infrastructure rather than separate systems.

At the inauguration of the new European Security and Strategy programme at the College of Europe in Natolin, EU Commissioner Andrius Kubilius called for a European Defence Union and Security Council. He outlined a new security architecture within NATO, responding to Russia’s military expansion, shifting US priorities and Ukraine’s strategic role.
Ten key takeaways
- Russia’s military expansion threatens European security. Kubilius warns that Russia is preparing for prolonged confrontation, with military spending projected at €180 billion in 2027, a 33% increase. In purchasing power parity terms, he estimates Russian defence expenditure could match the EU’s combined spending of €500–550 billion. He also warns that Russia could eventually deploy 10 million drones annually.
- NATO 3.0 requires Europeans to assume primary responsibility for conventional defence. As the United States increasingly redirects strategic resources towards the Indo-Pacific in response to China’s growing military and economic power, Europeans must take responsibility for their territorial defence. Kubilius expects the US to retain a secondary conventional role and maintain its nuclear umbrella.
- Europe needs a new security architecture within 10–15 years. Kubilius advocates a fundamental transformation from a predominantly transatlantic defence system towards European collective defence. His proposed Europe 3.0 concept would establish defence as a core dimension of European integration alongside the free movement of people and goods.
- A European Defence Union and Security Council could transform decision-making. Kubilius supports Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal for a European Security Council involving partners such as Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the United Kingdom. He envisages a European Defence Union anchored in Article 42(7) TEU, providing a stronger European pillar within NATO that is separable but not separate from the Alliance.
- China and India could fundamentally reshape the global economic order. Kubilius anticipates that China and India could become the world’s two largest economies by the end of the century, potentially pushing the United States into third place and the EU into fourth. He describes this as a historic reversal of the economic balance between East and West, requiring Europe to adapt its geopolitical strategy.
- A stronger EU-US strategic partnership could preserve Western influence. Kubilius argues that neither Europe nor the United States can independently prevent the relative economic rise of China and India. He proposes a new phase of Westernization, bringing Europe and America into a more integrated strategic community capable of maintaining global economic, technological and geopolitical influence.
- Russia’s long-term transformation is essential for lasting European peace. Kubilius considers Russia’s future the most unpredictable among the major geopolitical powers. Continued authoritarian aggression could lead to economic decline, instability or even state collapse. He argues that sustainable European security ultimately requires Russia to become a peaceful, responsible state, while rejecting an unconditional reset with President Vladimir Putin.
- Ukraine’s military victory and EU integration could encourage political change in Russia. Kubilius identifies three European instruments for influencing Russia’s long-term trajectory: supporting Ukraine’s military success, enabling its economic and social development through EU integration, and establishing a future framework for EU-Russia relations. Renewed economic cooperation with Russia should depend on its abandonment of aggressive policies.
- Poland, Germany and Ukraine could become the backbone of European defence. Kubilius proposes a strategic defence pillar centred on Poland, Germany and Ukraine, complemented by the Nordic and Baltic countries. Within NATO 3.0 and Europe 3.0, this regional configuration would form a central component of Europe’s future collective defence architecture, strengthening the continent’s eastern security capabilities.
- European integration must overcome national fragmentation. Kubilius argues that Europe’s ability to address major geopolitical transformations depends on collective ambition rather than competing national priorities. He calls for an intellectual transformation alongside financial, industrial and institutional reforms, urging a new generation of European leaders to develop the ideas needed for a more sovereign, united and strategically capable European Union.

high_priority_articles.summary: Ceasefire along front lines and lifting of sanctions against russia: WP columnist reveals details of US and European peace plan  Ukrainian news
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The United States and European countries are developing a joint peace plan for Ukraine. It calls for a freeze in hostilities along the front lines, a phased lifting of sanctions against russia, large-scale investments in Ukraine’s reconstruction, and security guarantees for the country. Columnist David Ignatius wrote about this in a column for The Washington Post, citing sources. He believes the plan is a “territorial compromise neither side will like,” but that a package of accompanying measures should make it more acceptable to both.
According to Ignatius, the “diplomatic push” occurred last Friday during a six-hour meeting in Florida. The meeting was attended by US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, as well as representatives from Ukraine, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany. One US official explained the logic behind the approach.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the columnist quotes him as saying.
According to Ignatius, a condition for implementing the initiative is the cessation of Ukrainian strikes on russian oil refineries.
What the peace plan offers russia?
Putin is being offered not only to end the war but also to conclude an economic and security agreement with Europe. It must take into account russia’s “security concerns,” although, as the columnist notes, it is not yet clear exactly what that will entail. Another element could be an energy agreement between russia, Ukraine, and Europe. One option is a pipeline to supply russian oil and gas to Europe, with profits shared between Ukraine and russia. The peace agreement should also specify which sanctions against russia will be lifted and when.
What security guarantees will Ukraine receive?
Under the plan, the US and European countries are to pledge a military response to Ukraine in the event of a new russian attack. According to a US official, such commitments would be equivalent to Article 5 of the NATO Charter on collective defense.
Who will finance Ukraine’s reconstruction?
The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock are to establish a special mechanism for post-war reconstruction. The funds are intended to be used for rebuilding destroyed areas, providing compensation to the families of fallen and wounded soldiers, and reviving the economy. US negotiators have already asked the Ukrainian side to provide a detailed cost estimate and guarantees of transparent use of the funds.
What the plan entails regarding territories?
The key and most contentious point is a freeze on hostilities along the current front line. According to the columnist, russia must agree to a ceasefire along the line of contact, while Ukraine must recognize russia’s control over the occupied territories. One of the obstacles remains the uncertainty regarding exactly where this line runs.
The column was published amid a public conflict between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy over a deal to supply diesel fuel. Ignatius notes that more than a year and a half ago, Trump claimed that Zelenskyy “has no cards" to play, yet now he is protesting Ukraine’s devastating strikes on russian oil refineries.
It is worth noting that russia had previously refused to end the war without control over the entire Donbas, while Ukraine ruled out officially recognizing russian control over the occupied territories.

South Korean chip stocks dropped sharply on Thursday, October 15, as investors reassessed the earnings outlook for the artificial intelligence industry and the risks surrounding global semiconductor investment.
Intraday reports showed SK Hynix falling around 11%, while Samsung Electronics declined roughly 9%–10%. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi fell about 8% during the session. These figures represent reported intraday moves rather than confirmed closing prices.
The declines formed part of a wider retreat in Asian technology shares following weakness on Wall Street. For South Korea, the selling highlighted how closely market sentiment has become tied to the performance of its largest semiconductor businesses.
The central question is whether rapid AI infrastructure spending can sustain the growth in chip demand and profitability that investors have anticipated.
The selloff does not, by itself, establish that demand for AI chips has weakened. Share prices reflect expectations about future earnings, which can change before orders or revenue show a clear slowdown.
Investors must assess several moving parts: how much cloud providers will continue spending, whether those investments generate adequate returns, and how quickly chipmakers can increase production.
Strong demand can support rising sales while still leaving stocks vulnerable if valuations already assume exceptional growth. Higher interest rates can add pressure by reducing the present value investors assign to future profits and increasing financing costs across the AI investment chain.
Product differences also matter. High-bandwidth memory used alongside AI accelerators, conventional DRAM and NAND flash storage serve different functions. Their pricing and competitive conditions can diverge, making broad claims about a single “memory cycle” less useful than examining each business separately.
A separate development has brought export restrictions back into focus.
Reports citing people familiar with the discussions indicate that SK Hynix’s US subsidiary, Solidigm, is seeking permission to install additional American chipmaking equipment at the group’s Dalian facility in China. The reported proposal links that expansion to plans for a new NAND flash memory factory in the United States.
Additional Chinese production could help generate funding for the proposed US investment. However, the discussions remain unconfirmed by the companies, and the equipment request should not be treated as an approved expansion.
The situation illustrates the competing pressures facing multinational chipmakers. Washington wants additional semiconductor manufacturing investment in the United States while restricting equipment shipments that could expand Chinese production.
For investors, the implications depend on the eventual licensing terms, construction commitments and funding requirements. The reported negotiations do not establish that export restrictions caused Thursday’s share-price declines.
South Korea’s latest trade figures provide a stronger picture of current semiconductor demand than the stock-market performance alone suggests.
Official figures show September semiconductor exports reached $60.30 billion, up 262.8% from a year earlier. The government linked the increase to expanding export volumes and higher contract prices as memory demand continued to grow.
Those figures cover total semiconductor exports. They should not be presented as memory-only sales or substituted directly for the unverified $37.59 billion figure in the original brief.
The contrast between strong exports and falling shares is significant. Export data describe business already taking place, while equity prices incorporate expectations about future supply, margins and growth.
Investors can therefore acknowledge robust current trading conditions while becoming more cautious about how long unusually favourable conditions will last.
New factories could support higher shipment volumes and strengthen manufacturers’ competitive positions. They could also put pressure on pricing if production eventually grows faster than demand.
A potential supply increase around 2029 should be treated as a risk scenario rather than a confirmed turning point. Construction schedules, equipment installation, manufacturing yields and customer qualification will determine when planned capacity becomes commercially available.
The effect will also depend on the products being manufactured. Additional NAND capacity would not necessarily resolve shortages in advanced high-bandwidth memory.
For South Korea, dependence on a small number of major exporters creates another consideration: changes in semiconductor sentiment can have an outsized effect on the domestic equity market.
Upcoming company updates will help investors compare market concerns with actual business conditions. Important indicators include memory contract prices, order commitments, inventory levels, capital expenditure and expected returns from new facilities.
Developments in US equipment licensing could also influence the timing and cost of SK Hynix’s expansion plans.
South Korea’s chip selloff reflects growing uncertainty about future returns from the AI investment boom. Strong exports remain a source of support, but sustained confidence will depend on whether demand, pricing and cash generation can keep pace with expanding production and investment.

high_priority_articles.summary: Elon Musk’s China RAM Warning Raises Questions for Samsung, SK Hynix as South Korea Faces Potential Memory Chip Oversupply and Less Time To Diversify  TradingView
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Elon Musk warned that China will be “making a lot” of random-access memory (RAM) by 2028, amplifying concerns that a future chip glut could expose South Korea’s dependence on Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. SSNLF and SK Hynix Inc. SKHY.
Musk Flags China’s Growing Memory Chip Output
"China will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028," Musk wrote Thursday on X, responding to P Equity Research’s summary of a South Korean column. The column warned that new capacity could cause oversupply in 2029 and argued Korea has two to three years to develop alternative growth industries.
China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies, aka CXMT, said in September its fifth-generation DRAM platform had entered mass production. Reuters reported that the company says its process can produce at least 50% more gross chip dies per wafer than its predecessor, underscoring China’s growing manufacturing capabilities.
South Korea’s Chip Dependence Raises Economic Risks
Reuters reported that CXMT held about 7.7% of the global DRAM market in 2025. However, it trails Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron in high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. Musk previously acknowledged China’s manufacturing scale but said advanced memory "will be harder to solve."
South Korea’s government reported that September semiconductor exports jumped 263% to $60.3 billion, nearly half of its record $120.9 billion in total exports. Any future reversal in chip prices could therefore hit national export earnings.
Samsung And SK Hynix Face Market Uncertainty
Gartner expects memory to generate $837 billion, or 54% of worldwide semiconductor revenue, in 2026, up from 27% in 2025. It forecasts tight supplies through 2027. SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung told Reuters in July that demand could exceed supply beyond 2030.
Samsung shares fell 9.5% and SK Hynix lost 11.1% Thursday, Reuters reported, amid a wider technology selloff driven by U.S. inflation concerns and doubts over AI investment. The declines followed earlier market jitters over China’s chipmaking advances.
